newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Heads to roll in French insurer row. [CORRECTED 20:28 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Heads to roll in French insurer row. [CORRECTED 20:28 GMT]

text.p: The French government on Monday called on the head of state insurer GAN to quit after it last week abandoned an attempt to privatise GAN banking subsidiary CIC, and it criticised the chairmen of both groups for failing to promote the sell-off.
(Corrects to make clear that it was the French government, not the GAN chief, which last week abandoned an attempt to privatise.)

The government's wrath over the privatisation failure looked set to claim both GAN chairman Jean-Jacques Bonnaud and Bernard Yoncourt, chairman of its profitable Credit Industriel et Commercial (CIC) regional banking subsidiary.
"The government has asked for the resignation of Mr Jean-Jacques Bonnaud," a finance ministry spokeswoman said.

The request adds a new twist to a tale of tortured government relations with GAN after conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe tried early this year to place a close advisor, Pierre-Mathieu Duhamel, as head of CIC. He backed off amid a storm of media controversy, paving the way for Yoncourt'a appointment.
A source close to the case said the new GAN chairman would then appoint a new boss at CIC, but declined to give any names. Bonnaud's replacement will likely be named next week.
"The new chairman of GAN will name a new head of CIC," the source said.
Neither GAN, whose full name is Groupe des Assurances Nationales, nor CIC would make any immediate comment.

Other sources said after the decision, taken in consultation with the prime minister, of naming a successor would have to wait until after the return of French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis at the end of the week. He is in Japan on a visit with President Jacques Chirac.
Yoncourt infuriated Arthuis in October after declaring on television that the sale of CIC to a major French bank could spell "death" for the banking group.

Arthuis said at the time he would "draw the consequences" of Yoncourt's "unacceptable" behaviour and made it clear last week when announcing the cancellation of the CIC privatisation tender that Bonnaud, who is ultimately responsible for CIC as part of the GAN group, was also in the firing line.
"The managers of GAN and CIC did not behave in a way to encourage progress in this process," he said last week.

The government received only two bids for CIC, a profitable grouping of 11 regional banks whose clients are mainly big and medium sized companies -- from Banque Nationale de Paris (BNP) and Societe Generale.

The French privatisation commission rejected the offer from Societe Generale on the grounds it did not comply with the terms imposed by the government, of which the most important is that any buyer must preserve the bank's regional integrity.
Arthuis said he was determined to privatise the group but that he was breaking off a tender in which there was only one eligible offer on the table to take more time to reflect.
Staff and trade unions opposed the sell-off with strikes and protests over feared job losses but the spectre of a break-up of the group also sparked widespread fears among local politicians.
The government's options appear limited as long as it sticks to the strict conditions for all potential buyers.

Two possibilities suggested by banking analysts and the media after the privatisation tender was cancelled are a rerun in which the savings bank group Caisse d'Epargne could also enter the bidding and some form of coordinated takeover of each of the 11 regional banks which would keep the grouping intact.

CIC has a value of around 14 billion francs ($2.7 billion) on GAN's books, which would correspond to about 9.4 billion francs for the 67 percent which the government had offered for sale in the now defunct tender. 3($=5.0955 french francs)
